faqs.question: How do you pronounce "Ich vermisse dich"?
faqs.answer: Roughly ikh fair-MISS-uh dikh. Duden marks the stress on the second syllable of vermissen, and both instances of -ch here are the soft front ch, closer to the h in "huge" than to a k.

faqs.question: Is it "Ich vermisse dich" or "Ich vermisse dir"?
faqs.answer: Always dich. DWDS lists vermissen with an accusative object (mit Akkusativobjekt: die Mutter, den Vater, die Familie, Freunde vermissen), and dir is dative. Ich vermisse dir is simply ungrammatical.

faqs.question: What does "Du fehlst mir" literally mean in English?
faqs.answer: "You are missing, to me." Du is the nominative subject and mir a dative experiencer, so the person missed is the grammatical subject. DWDS glosses this sense of fehlen as sehr vermisst, entbehrt werden — to be greatly missed.

faqs.question: Can I say "Du fehlst mich"?
faqs.answer: No. Fehlen takes a dative, never an accusative, so it is du fehlst mir. This is the single most common mistake English speakers make with the construction, because English has no case ending to warn them.

faqs.question: How do I say "I miss you" to my German boss?
faqs.answer: Ich vermisse Sie, with a capital S mid-sentence. Sie is the formal address and you keep it for anyone you do not already call du. Sending the du form upward reads as presumptuous rather than warm.

faqs.question: How do I say "I miss you" to more than one person?
faqs.answer: Ich vermisse euch, where euch is the accusative of the plural ihr — for a family, a group of friends or a team. It is attested as Tatoeba sentence 385357 and turns up 35 times in the DWDS subtitle corpus.

faqs.question: How do I say "I missed you" about the past?
faqs.answer: Ich habe dich vermisst, the perfect tense, which is what Germans actually use in speech rather than the simple past. It returns 297 hits in the DWDS subtitle corpus, against 105 for the fehlen equivalent du hast mir gefehlt.

faqs.question: How do I say "I miss you so much" in German?
faqs.answer: Ich vermisse dich so sehr, or Ich vermisse dich sehr for the plainer version. The plain one is attested as Tatoeba sentence 607221; the so sehr version has no Tatoeba sentence but 25 occurrences in the subtitle corpus.

faqs.question: Does "Du fehlst" on its own mean "I miss you"?
faqs.answer: No, and this is worth knowing. Without the dative, DWDS gives fehlen the sense abwesend sein — to be absent, as in er hat zwei Tage unentschuldigt gefehlt. Du fehlst alone says you were marked absent.

faqs.question: Do I need a German keyboard to type these lines?
faqs.answer: No. Neither Ich vermisse dich nor Du fehlst mir contains an umlaut or an ß, so an ordinary English keyboard types both exactly. You only need the special characters for words like Nähe or müssen.

faqs.question: How do I reply when someone writes "Ich vermisse dich"?
faqs.answer: Ich vermisse dich auch — "I miss you too" — which returns 80 hits in the DWDS subtitle corpus. If they wrote the other construction, mirror it back as Du fehlst mir auch, which returns 32.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ich Vermisse Dich or Du Fehlst Mir: Saying I Miss You in German

To say **i miss you in German**, write **Ich vermisse dich**. An English speaker can build it word for word — *ich* nominative, *vermissen* the verb, *dich* accusative object, in that order. The second construction, **Du fehlst mir**, does invert: "you are missing to me". Which is more common is asserted on every page about this and counted on none, so this one counted: across 75,520,701 words of German film dialogue in the [DWDS Filmuntertitel corpus](https://www.dwds.de/d/korpora/untertitel), *ich vermisse dich* returns 453 hits to 232 for *du fehlst mir*. Below: what Germany's reference dictionaries say about the pair, the *dich* / *Sie* / *euch* decision that can genuinely offend, and what 214 "I miss you" pages built on SubhSandesh since 2026-07-28 show about the letter around the line — a median of 88 words, 43.5% locked behind a password.

## What "Ich vermisse dich" literally says

*Vermissen* is a weak transitive verb taking an accusative object. [DWDS](https://www.dwds.de/wb/vermissen) gives its principal parts as *vermisst, vermisste, hat vermisst* and defines its first sense as being aware with regret that someone is no longer near you, and feeling it as a personal lack.

Its collocation block is the useful part: **mit Akkusativobjekt: die Mutter, den Vater, die Familie, Freunde vermissen.** The objects German corpora attach to this verb are people.

*Dich* is the accusative of *du*, so the shape is identical to English: I — miss — you. French *tu me manques* and Italian *mi manchi* swap the roles, and Spanish offers three constructions; sibling posts cover those. German asks you to re-map nothing, and Pfeifer's etymology on that same DWDS page explains why: *missen* and English *to miss* descend from one Germanic root.

One trap. In the passive, *vermisst* is the missing-persons word: DWDS lists *Besatzungsmitglieder, Passagiere, Bergleute werden vermisst*, crew and miners *reported missing*. *Ich vermisse dich* is affectionate; *Du wirst vermisst* is a police notice.

## Du fehlst mir, and what the dictionaries say about it

*Fehlen* is the second construction and it genuinely inverts: *du* is nominative, the one missing, and *mir* a dative experiencer. *Du fehlst mich* is the commonest error; the verb never takes an accusative.

Now the part no page on this subject prints. [DWDS defines the person-sense of *fehlen*](https://www.dwds.de/wb/fehlen) — sense 1b, ⟨jmd. fehlt jmdm.⟩ — as **sehr vermisst, entbehrt werden**, "to be greatly missed": it defines *fehlen* using *vermissen*. [Duden does the same](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/fehlen), glossing its fourth sense *[sehnlich] herbeigewünscht, vermisst werden*.

Neither defines *vermissen* in terms of *fehlen*. The direction runs one way, making *vermissen* the primitive and this sense of *fehlen* the derived one — and both glosses smuggle in an intensifier, *sehr* and *sehnlich*. What the dictionaries encode is strength, not warmth.

DWDS then prints, as its illustrative quotation for that sense, a line from a 2022 collection of text-message phrases: *"Ich vermisse dich, du fehlst mir, komm bitte zurück."* Both constructions, one sentence, *vermissen* first — Germans use them together, not as rivals.

German dative-experiencer verbs are also less rigid than the textbook suggests. Somers, Jenset and Barðdal's 2024 study in *Lingua*, on 200 corpus tokens for each of fourteen alternating verbs, found that apparent dative-first verbs such as *gefallen* run nominative-first 58% of the time. *Fehlen* is not in their set, so that describes the class rather than this sentence — but it is why the "inverted" line still starts with *du*.

The trap with *fehlen* is what it does without the dative. DWDS sense 2a, ⟨jmd. fehlt⟩, is simply *abwesend sein* — *er hat zwei Tage unentschuldigt gefehlt*. **Du fehlst mir** is tender; **Du fehlst** alone means you were marked absent.

## Is "du fehlst mir" really more common? 75 million words say no

That *du fehlst mir* is both more common and warmer is repeated on every page ranking for this phrase. Half of it is testable.

The DWDS Filmuntertitel corpus is built from the German side of opensubtitles.org: 11,993 documents, 75,520,701 tokens, all classified as spoken register. It is the closest publicly countable thing to a transcript of German talk.

Counted there, *ich vermisse dich* returns 453 hits and *du fehlst mir* 232; restricted to the exact present-tense string, 410 to 223. The gap survives every variation tested: 297 for *ich habe dich vermisst* to 105 for *du hast mir gefehlt*, and 80 for the reply *ich vermisse dich auch* to 32 for *du fehlst mir auch*. DWDS's 107-million-token blog collection agrees at 25 to 12.

Where the count goes the other way it is too small to mean anything: 3 to 6 in the 20th-century DWDS-Kernkorpus, 3 to 9 in the historical Deutsches Textarchiv. Literary German may well have preferred *fehlen*; six hits cannot establish it.

Three limits, stated rather than buried. Subtitle dialogue over-represents intimacy, so it shows which form dominates *this kind of sentence*, not German as a whole. "Warmer" is not a countable property at all, so this page drops that half of the claim rather than restating it. And lemma counts do not help: *fehlen* has 7,740,436 hits to *vermissen*'s 1,172,332 across DWDS's 53.4-billion-token set, but *fehlen* mostly means "to be lacking", as in *es fehlt an Geld*.

| German line | What it literally says | Hits in 75.5M words | Fit on a miss-you page |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich vermisse dich | I miss you | 410 | Headline line; 86.4% of 214 pages carry a memory |
| Du fehlst mir | You are missing to me | 223 | Opens a letter; median 88 words |
| Ich habe dich vermisst | I have missed you | 297 | A reunion; 28.0% set a reunion date |
| Ich vermisse dich so sehr | I miss you so much | 25 | A voice note; 13.6% record one |
| Ich vermisse Sie | I miss you, formal | 9 | Rarely right here |

Read the last row twice: nine against 410. Film dialogue is overwhelmingly between intimates, which tells you about the corpus, not your inbox.

## dich, Sie or euch — the choice that can actually offend

German makes you declare the relationship in the pronoun. There is no neutral option, and sending a *du* form upward is a social error, not a stylistic one.

### Ich vermisse dich — informal, one person

For a partner, a sibling, a close friend, anyone you already address as *du*. Attested on [Tatoeba as sentence 110](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/110), translated "I miss you" and "I pine for you". This is the form with 410 corpus hits.

### Ich vermisse Sie — formal, one person or several

Capital *Sie* mid-sentence is the formal address: a manager, a teacher, a partner's parents who have not offered *du*. Attested as Tatoeba sentence 385356. If you use *Sie* elsewhere, do not drop it here because it feels warmer; it reads as presumption.

### Ich vermisse euch — informal, more than one person

*Euch* is the accusative of *ihr*, the plural *du*: a family, a group of friends, a team. Attested as Tatoeba sentence 385357, with 35 subtitle-corpus occurrences. The *fehlen* counterparts, *Sie fehlen mir* and *Ihr fehlt mir*, have no exact Tatoeba sentence, so they are named rather than recommended.

## What people search, what is attested, and what hijacks the phrase

*Ich vermisse dich sehr* is the safe strengthener: Tatoeba sentence 607221, carrying six English translations from "very much" to "dearly", and matching Duden's own example *den Freund sehr vermissen*. *Du fehlst mir sehr* is sentence 527924.

*Ich vermisse dich so sehr* has no exact Tatoeba sentence but 25 subtitle-corpus occurrences, so the corpus stands behind it here. *Du fehlst mir so sehr* has nine, as does *ich vermisse dich jetzt schon*.

Three lines drafted for this page were cut for returning **zero hits in 75.5 million words**: *ich vermisse dich schmerzlich*, *du gehst mir ab* and *mir fehlt deine Nähe*. DWDS's thesaurus panel already marks *schmerzlich vermissen* elevated and formulaic; the corpus confirms nobody says it to a person.

Expect one complication if you search the German phrase rather than the English: it is also a television title. German Wikipedia carries an article named exactly [*Ich vermisse dich*](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ich_vermisse_dich) — the Netflix series from Harlan Coben's *Missing You*, released 1 January 2025 under that German title. For the one-line version in fifty-odd other languages, [our hub on saying I miss you in different languages](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) carries the table; this page is the depth under its German row.

## What the page around the line does, and the limits of that data

Across 214 pages created on the [miss-you page for a partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) since that template went live on 2026-07-28, the median letter runs 88 words and the longest 1,024. Eighty-eight words is one screen: the German line, one memory, one sentence about when you next meet.

The number worth knowing before you write is the privacy one. 43.5% of miss-you senders password-protect the page before sharing — 93 of 214, against 38.5% platform-wide, the most private segment measured here. Recipients tapped a hug 1,434 times across 138 of the 214 pages, 512 on one page: a return signal a chat message never produces.

Three limits, plainly. The 47 city pairs these pages name, Berlin–London included, come from a **15-city picker with defaults** — not sender choices, so nothing about geography follows. The 2,417 recorded views are **page views, not unique visitors**: one recipient reopening a page twenty times counts twenty times. And n = 214 over two months supports no seasonal claim.

## When a German line is the wrong thing to send

If the person reads English comfortably and your German stops at this sentence, send the German line with an English letter under it. A whole phrasebook message compounds register errors, and the *Sie* / *du* slip is the one nobody will tell you about.

If what you are missing is daily rather than dramatic, this template is not the best fit either. *Fehlen* means something closer to "not sufficiently present", and one big page answers a different feeling. [Streak](https://subhsandesh.in/streak) — one tap a day each, every check-in keeping a word, a diary after a hundred days neither of you meant to write — suits the everyday version better.

And if you are in the same city this week, say it out loud. Nothing sent over a link competes with four syllables in person.

## Sources

- [DWDS — *vermissen*](https://www.dwds.de/wb/vermissen), Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache
- [DWDS — *fehlen*](https://www.dwds.de/wb/fehlen), Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache
- [Duden — *fehlen*](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/fehlen), Bibliographisches Institut
- [DWDS Filmuntertitel corpus](https://www.dwds.de/d/korpora/untertitel) — 11,993 documents, 75,520,701 tokens
- Somers, Jenset & Barðdal (2024), ["Subjecthood and argument structure of synonymous Dat-Nom/Nom-Dat verbs"](https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/01J96HWNJ856GF7QG8BT799BEV), *Lingua* 247:103833
- [Tatoeba — *Ich vermisse dich.*, sentence 110](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/110), CC BY 2.0 FR

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this SERP that cites a dictionary or counts a corpus, and both yield claims no competitor states: DWDS and Duden define fehlen's person-sense using vermissen and never the reverse, and ich vermisse dich outnumbers du fehlst mir 453 to 232 across 75.5 million words of German dialogue — which falsifies the "more common" half of the claim every competing page repeats, while the "warmer" half is dropped as untestable rather than restated. Add the dich/Sie/euch send-to rule, three lines cut for zero corpus hits, and recipient-side data nobody else measures, and there are four separate reasons to cite it. What it cannot overcome: fluentu.com and lingoda.com are established language-learning domains with years of topical links, while subhsandesh.in is a gifting site with no German-language authority, so an answer engine may cite this for the corpus point while Google still ranks them above it. Ranking, if it happens, takes months.

structuralLimitations: BRIEF §0 CORRECTION (raised mid-task by the orchestrator, and re-checked here) — the prompt said "a Harlan Coben Netflix series localised as Ich vermisse dich also contaminates the German head term". The orchestrator later flagged that a sibling agent had falsified the equivalent French claim and asked me not to assert a localised title on its say-so. I verified the German case independently through the MediaWiki and Wikidata APIs before printing anything: de.wikipedia carries an article titled exactly "Ich vermisse dich" with no redirect, its Wikidata item is Q124795248, its opening line reads "Ich vermisse dich (Originaltitel: Missing You) ist eine Fernsehserie, die auf dem gleichnamigen Buch von Harlan Coben beruht … am 1. Januar 2025 auf Netflix veröffentlicht", and Q124795248's German label is "Ich vermisse dich" with the enwiki sitelink "Missing You (2025 TV series)". So the claim holds for German, and the post states it with the German Wikipedia article as the link. The French sibling's finding does not transfer: it concerns a French article that does not exist and Q67960905, a 2019 Bolivian film, neither of which bears on the German title.

BRIEF §1 COMPLIANCE — what I did NOT claim. The prompt's SERP context was for the German-language sibling query `ich vermisse dich sprüche`, not for `ich vermisse dich`. I never ran a German-market SERP, so the first draft's line that the series "now occupies much of that result page" was cut and replaced with the entity fact alone. The post makes no claim about what ranks on any German-language SERP.

PROMPT CLAIM TESTED AND FALSIFIED IN PART — the prompt asked me to test rather than assert that du fehlst mir is "warmer" or "more common" than ich vermisse dich, and said DWDS corpus data could answer it. It can, with one correction to the method. DWDS's public frequency API explicitly refuses multi-word expressions ("Für Mehrwortausdrücke … ist diese Angabe nicht verfügbar"), so lemma frequency is the only thing it returns: fehlen 7,740,436 hits to vermissen's 1,172,332 over 53,362,074,529 tokens. That number is worthless here, because fehlen's dominant senses are shortage and absence. The answerable route is DWDS's public DDC/dstar corpus endpoint, and it gives the opposite of the folklore: ich vermisse dich 453 to du fehlst mir 232 in the 75.5M-token Filmuntertitel corpus, 25 to 12 in the 107M-token blogs corpus. The "more common" claim is false in every contemporary corpus large enough to test it. The "warmer" claim is not testable by counting at all and was dropped rather than repeated.

WHERE THE EVIDENCE GOES THE OTHER WAY, AND WHY IT IS NOT USED TO CLAIM ANYTHING — in the DWDS-Kernkorpus (20th century) the counts are 3 to 6, in Kernkorpus 21 2 to 3, and in the Deutsches Textarchiv 3 to 9, all favouring du fehlst mir. Single digits support no claim in either direction, and the post says so instead of quietly reporting only the corpora that agree with it.

METHOD NOTE ON THE COUNTS — a DDC quoted string is case-insensitive and expands inflection, so "ich vermisse dich" also returns Ich vermisste dich and Ich vermiss dich. Every figure printed as a form count was re-derived from the returned KWIC surface strings, not from the raw hit total; that is where 410 (present-tense exact) against the 453 raw total comes from. The same re-derivation separated capital Sie (9, formal address) from lowercase sie (114, her/them) inside the 129 raw hits for "ich vermisse sie", which a raw count would have conflated.

LINE CUT 1 — ich vermisse dich schmerzlich. Zero hits in 75,520,701 words, and DWDS's own openThesaurus panel marks schmerzlich vermissen "geh." and "floskelhaft" (elevated, formulaic). Cut as a line to send; kept in the body only as an example of a cut.

LINE CUT 2 — du gehst mir ab, the Austrian/Bavarian variant. Zero hits in the subtitle corpus and no entry fetched from DWDS or Duden to stand behind it. Cut rather than printed on a competitor's authority.
LINE CUT 3 — mir fehlt deine Nähe ("I miss your closeness"). Zero hits. Cut.

LINE CUT 4 — Sie fehlen mir and Ihr fehlt mir, the fehlen counterparts of the formal and plural forms. No exact Tatoeba sentence for either, and the quoted-string corpus counts for them are unusable because DDC conflates the ihr/sie lemma (both queries return the identical 69-hit set). They are named in the body as existing, never recommended as lines to send.

LINE CUT 5 — ich vermiss dich voll, the colloquial intensifier. The bare ich vermiss dich is attested (31 occurrences), but the voll variant was not verified against any fetched source, so the whole line was cut rather than assembled from an attested half.

LINE CUT 6 — an IPA transcription for vermissen. DWDS's pronunciation field on that entry returns an error and prints no IPA, so the FAQ gives Duden's stress marking (verm-I-ssen) and a plain-English approximation instead of an IPA string I would have had to invent. DWDS does print [ˈfeːlən] for fehlen, which is why only that verb could have carried one.

LINE CUT 7 — the claim that ich vermisse dich so sehr is "standard". It has no exact Tatoeba sentence, only 25 subtitle-corpus occurrences, and the post says which source stands behind it rather than implying both do.

LINE CUT 8 — a sentence contrasting German with French, Italian and Spanish at length. Cut to one clause on the BRIEF's instruction not to re-explain sibling posts' grammar; the contrast survives as a single sentence naming tu me manques and mi manchi without analysing them.

WHAT THIS DOES THAT THE HUB DOES NOT — the live hub /blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages (Strapi id 1360) gives German exactly one line: "German: Ich vermisse dich (ikh fer-MIS-uh dikh)". It never mentions du fehlst mir, carries no register information, and cites nothing. Its table is not restated here. This page adds the second construction, both dictionary entries, the corpus count, the dich/Sie/euch rule, the fehlen-without-dative trap, the vermisst missing-persons trap, and the first-party channel data — German-specific depth a fifty-language table cannot carry.

CANNIBALISATION — of the 1,200 live slugs pulled from Strapi on 2026-09-25, zero contain "german" or "deutsch", and none of the 81 live "miss" slugs is a translation spoke for any European language (the live spokes are Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali, Punjabi, Gujarati and Urdu). On the BRIEF's three-axis test this differs on the language axis from every one of them. No merge recommended.

PEER-REVIEWED SOURCE, AND ITS HONEST LIMIT — Somers, Jenset & Barðdal (2024) in Lingua was fetched in full as the green open-access copy from Ghent University and read, not cited from an abstract. Its German verb set is dünken, gefallen, grauen, leidtun, zufallen, entgehen, genügen, geziemen, nützen and reichen. fehlen is not among them, so the paper is cited for what German dative-experiencer verbs do as a class and the post says so in the same sentence. findpapers.mjs was run on all three suggested queries; the closest German-specific alternative (Proost, "The argument structure of psych-verbs", IDS Mannheim, doi:10.1515/9783110457155-002) is green OA but its repository served an anti-bot challenge, and an unreadable source is not a citable one.

SERP LIMIT — five of the nine results were fetchable and were parsed programmatically for headings, table count, FAQPage markup and any occurrence of dwds.de, duden.de or "corpus": fluentu.com (2,166 words), lingoda.com (1,817), memrise.com (674), deutschgym.com (250), learnwitholiver.com (131). None carries a table, FAQ markup, a dictionary citation or a corpus count. Pinterest, Quora and the DeepL permalink were not analysed. No competing page is linked, cited or paraphrased anywhere in the post.

FIRST-PARTY LIMIT — /missyou-gf letter text is free input and is not language-tagged, so the platform cannot say how many of the 214 senders wrote any German at all. The table's fourth column is therefore about the channel and the page's own fields, never about which German line anyone used, and the body does not imply otherwise.

TEMPLATE CHOICE — /missyou-gf is batch-mandatory and is also where the first-party data comes from. The alternative is /streak, chosen on merit rather than availability: fehlen's core sense is "not sufficiently present", a daily low-grade absence, and /streak is the only template in oneOfLinks built for a repeated rather than a one-shot message. /dedication (already in four posts) and /catch (two) were passed over as over-used in this batch and less apt for this reader.
